_comment: Zork I, measured — not estimated. Produced by replaying the verified 350-point
walkthrough through @folio/zmachine and observing the World State Contract every
Read the scale-free ratios, not the absolute counts. Zork has 82 rooms because
Zork is Zork; a game adapted from a short story should not be held to that. What
transfers between games of different sizes is the SHAPE: how interconnected the
map is, how much of the world is load-bearing, how often the game pays out, and
how long it dares to make you wait.

readings.loopsPerRoom: 0.67 loops per room is the number that most sharply separates a real adventure map from a generated one. Zork's map is emphatically not a tree: 82 rooms carry 136 connections, so nearly every room sits on a circuit. That is what lets a player build a mental model, take a shortcut, and feel the map as a place rather than a menu.
readings.takeRate: Only 43% of objects the player ever sees end up carried. The majority of Zork's world is scenery, and deliberately so — a world where everything is takeable reads as a shopping list. Scenery is what makes the takeable things feel chosen.
readings.movesPerScoreEvent: A reward roughly every 11-12 moves across a 493-move game. Fast enough to keep faith, slow enough that arriving somewhere means something.
readings.longestDrySpell: 69 moves — fully 14% of the game — with no reward at all. This is the single most surprising number in the profile, and the most instructive: a classic asks for far more patience than a modern designer would dare. A generated game tuned to reward constantly would feel less like Zork, not more.
readings.pacingQuartiles: Points earned per quarter of the run: 85 / 104 / 71 / 90. Remarkably even, with a dip in the third quarter — the mid-game slog before the endgame pays out. Not a difficulty ramp; a rhythm.
